extracted.intended_audience: readers and contributors of The Spectator; general literate public interested in essays, moral criticism, and social advice (early-18th-century readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Producing and reading short moral and critical essays, letters, translations and satires in The Spectator (early 18th‑century periodical). Includes guidance on prayer, satire, translation fidelity, theatrical taste, church music, and social etiquette.

rubrics_metrics.name: Socrates' rules for prayer
rubrics_metrics.description: Threefold prescription for acceptable prayer drawn from Plato's Alcibiades: (1) Use a short, comprehensive prayer asking for things that are truly good for us (example: 'O Jupiter, give us those Things which are good for us, whether they are such Things as we pray for, or such Things as we do not pray for'); (2) Apply yourself to the study of true wisdom to know what is expedient; (3) Live in constant practice of your duty towards the gods and towards men (example: the Lacedaemonians' petition 'to give them all good Things so long as they were virtuous').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation: Men are often ignorant or biased and may pray for things that harm them; the best method to render prayers acceptable is to cultivate wisdom and virtue. The Christian form of prayer ('thy will be done') aligns with Socrates' first rule and is praised as humble and prudent. Additional explanation ties these rules to praying without ostentation, petitioning for the coming of God's kingdom, daily sustenance, and praying generally against sin, leaving particulars to divine omniscience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire should expose corrigible faults and discriminate
rubrics_metrics.description: A satiric piece (a 'Satyr') ought to 'expose nothing but what is corrigible, and make a due Discrimination between those who are, and those who are not the proper Objects of it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid levelling attacks that condemn an entire class or species (e.g., indicting all women or all humanity). Good satire targets faults that can be remedied and distinguishes between truly blameworthy subjects and those who are not proper objects of satire; indiscriminate or universal satirizing is 'of no Use to the World.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation fidelity: preserve the author's sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: When translating (example: Simonides' satyr), render the author's sentiments 'very faithfully'—not necessarily word-for-word when the language won't bear that, but so as 'to comprehend every one of his Sentiments, without adding any thing of my own.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translator should avoid adding personal material or altering the author's meaning; adjust literal wording only where necessary for the target language, and strive to communicate the full intent and spirit of the original while observing contemporary delicacy when required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe bienséance (decency) in allusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern practice requires observing what the French call the 'bienséance' in an allusion—i.e., mind the decency and propriety of comparisons and images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While ancient writers often used coarse or indecent comparisons without regard, contemporary writers/readers are expected to avoid indecent allusions; the rule of decency in comparisons is a recent refinement and should be followed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper theatrical aim and audience response: evoke pity, not mere laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy and elevated dramatic incidents should move pity and serious emotion rather than produce laughter or frivolous amusement (example criticism: the audience laughed at Lady Macbeth's astonishment and at a stabbing, which signals misplaced taste).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrights should craft incidents that engage the noble passions (pity, generosity) rather than merely stimulating appetites or coarse mirth. Audiences and social company should allow themselves legitimate feeling (tears, pity) without shame; excessive concern with appearances suppresses proper emotional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church music conformity: avoid divergent solo airs in congregation
rubrics_metrics.description: Singing the Psalms in a different tune from the congregation—introducing operatic airs or solo divisions while the congregation sings the plain tune—is improper and 'a Sort of Schism' (claimed not tolerated by the Toleration Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clergy and parishioners should discourage fashionable individuals from vocalising solo, operatic divisions over the congregational psalm tune; such departures make public worship appear as entertainment and risk spreading affectation through the parish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errata publication procedure (editorial correction)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a printing error is discovered, publish a precise erratum specifying the paper/date/column/line and the exact word correction (example: 'In the Paper of Saturday, Octob. 13, Col. 3. Line 11, for "Glass" read "Bottle"').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrections should be explicit and located so readers can verify the change. This is the proper method for remedying typographical mistakes noticed by readers or clubs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social-notification etiquette for persons 'in town'
rubrics_metrics.description: When someone comes to town they should notify acquaintances promptly (the complainant says if one does not visit within the week it becomes 'a mortal Quarrel'); suggested methods are 'put it in the Advertisement of your Paper' or 'order them to breathe their saucy Footmen' to inform acquaintances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely notification—within the first week of residence—is expected to prevent social misunderstandings. The periodical can serve as an accepted public channel (advertisement) for such notices; alternatively servants/footmen may be employed as a customary courtesy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and object of satirical discrimination (avoid universal condemnation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good satirist must make due discriminations and not 'expose the Sex in general' or 'endeavour to shew by some Superficial Strokes of Wit, that Brutes are the more excellent Creatures of the two.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire is most useful when it is targeted and just; broad-brush attacks on entire groups (sexes, mankind) are ineffective and unjust. The satirist should single out particular vices that can be corrected rather than leveling wholesale condemnation.
